name: Single-leg squat
pattern: One-leg squat: the standing hip, knee and ankle bend while the free leg is held off the floor.
setup: Stand on one leg, foot straight ahead, the other foot just off the floor in front.
Arms forward for balance, or hold a support.
Pick a box or bench behind you to sit to until you have the full range.

steps.text: Stand tall on one leg, hips level.
Sit back and down, knee over your middle toes, free leg reaching forward.
Go as low as you can control, from a 60° knee bend up to a full pistol.
Drive through your whole foot back to standing without leaning to the side.

cues.cue: Knee stays over your middle toes.
cues.why: Poor single-leg squatters showed weaker, later-firing hip abductors and more knee drift inward.

cues.cue: Hips level: do not let the free side drop.
cues.why: A dropping pelvis is the other sign of weak glute medius; the single-leg squat trains it well.

cues.cue: Lean forward as a unit, chest over the knee.
cues.why: A forward lean balances the free leg and brings the glutes into the lift.

cues.cue: Heel down, weight over the middle of the foot.
cues.why: Deep single-leg squats need about 35-40° of ankle bend; raise the heel slightly if you lack it.

cues.cue: Use a box and lower it over time.
cues.why: Depth you can control matters more than depth.

breathing: Breathe in on the way down, out as you stand.

tempo.note: Lower slowly, about 3 seconds; control is the point.

mistakes.name: Knee caves in
mistakes.looks: The knee falls inside the big toe as you go down.
mistakes.fix: Push the knee out over your little toe; shorten the range.
mistakes.why: Weak or late hip abductors; the main failure in the single-leg squat test.

mistakes.name: Hip drops
mistakes.looks: The free-leg side of the pelvis sinks and the trunk leans over the standing leg.
mistakes.fix: Keep your belt line level; squeeze the side of your standing hip.
mistakes.why: The glute medius is not holding the pelvis.

mistakes.name: Heel lifts
mistakes.looks: The standing heel rises and you tip forward at the bottom.
mistakes.fix: Stop higher, or put a small plate under the heel.
mistakes.why: Not enough ankle bend for the depth.

mistakes.name: Back rounds and falls back
mistakes.looks: At the bottom the lower back curls and you roll back onto the floor.
mistakes.fix: Reach your arms forward, use a counterweight, or sit to a box.
mistakes.why: The body's weight is behind the foot; rounding is the spine giving the missing range.

safety: Knee pain: stay in the range above the pain, often a 45-60° knee bend.
Balance: hold a rail, a strap or a doorway until you can control the descent.

variants.change: Hold a strap or support: less load, easier balance.
Sit to a box to set the depth.
Stand on a box with the free leg hanging down: full depth without the leg hitting the floor.
Weight held in front acts as a counterweight; easier to stay balanced.
Jump from the bottom and land on the same leg, soft knee.
Unstable surface: much harder balance, lighter range.

subtypes.name: Pistol squat
subtypes.change: Full depth, free leg straight out in front, held level.

subtypes.name: Shrimp squat
subtypes.change: Free knee bent behind you, hand holding that foot; lower until the back knee touches the floor.

subtypes.name: Single-leg wall sit
subtypes.change: Back on the wall, one foot on the floor with thigh level, other leg held straight out. Tracking: hold.

metrics.label: Knee inside the foot line (front view)

motion.basis: Standing leg is the right. Default is a single-leg squat to about 90° knee bend (clinical tests use 45-60°, crossley2011, ugalde2015). Pistol bottom angles estimated from the needed knee, hip and ankle range; not measured in these sources.
